description: Not42 is a team of BSc Physics graduates from Nepal, passionate about physics, rocket science, and space exploration. We aim to use science, technology, and NASA data to build meaningful solutions for humanity's future. Our interests include astrophysics, astronomy, AI/ML, scientific computing, and space technology.
summary:
Blinkit (team Not42) turns real NASA SPHEREx sky visits into an accessible flipbook to spot what moved or changed over time. It provides time-ordered blinking, WiseView-style color composites, ±5σ difference maps, and Gaia DR3 motion verification. We also began exploring "Six Eyes" to prototype multi-detector deep stacks and coarse spectral trends across bands.

Try it: 
https://blinkit.study (primary) ·
https://aws.blinkit.study (AWS backup) ·
Code: https://github.com/kripas1369/blinkit (branch phase1-complete)

The challenge asks how SPHEREx's time-domain scans can uncover hidden movers like cold brown dwarfs and Planet X candidates. Handling raw 62 MB FITS files with variable filter wavelengths is daunting. Blinkit solves this by streaming small pixel cutouts in seconds, aligning visits onto a common grid, and vetting candidates against optical and infrared catalogs.

We see this hackathon as our foundation, not the finish line. Much remains to be done—especially refining multi-detector coadds, spectral extraction, and automated candidate vetting. Blinkit provides an honest, transparent tool that we will keep developing and proving as SPHEREx continues surveying the dynamic universe.
details:
What it does and how it works?

We built Blinkit to bring the simple thrill of watching the sky move into anyone’s browser. When you pick a target like Barnard’s Star or type any celestial coordinates (RA/Dec), Blinkit gathers real NASA SPHEREx visits of that exact patch of sky and turns them into an interactive flipbook. You can blink back and forth across different observation dates, switch through detector arrays D1–D6, or view multi-epoch color composites where past and present visits blend into vivid blue and red trails. We also added difference maps that isolate moving objects and cross-matched every view with Gaia DR3 and CatWISE catalogs so you can immediately see if a moving dot matches known physics or a known star. Behind the scenes, instead of forcing people to download giant 62 MB FITS files, our backend uses HTTP byte-range requests to stream only the tiny slice of pixels needed directly from AWS S3, aligns them onto a shared sky grid, and delivers ready-to-view frames in seconds.

What benefits it has?

Most people don't have specialized astronomy software, heavy workstations, or the coding background needed to parse raw telescope files. Blinkit brings all of that into an intuitive, zero-install web interface. It saves massive bandwidth by pulling only the pixels you look at (~1 MB instead of 62 MB), stays honest about instrument flaws by highlighting bad pixels rather than hiding them, and encodes your exact view, speed, and filter settings into a shareable URL so you can easily send discoveries to a classmate, teammate, or teacher.

What the intended impact of the project is?

A decade ago, a grassroots tool called WiseView empowered citizen scientists to discover hundreds of cold brown dwarfs and asteroids hidden in WISE survey data. SPHEREx is now mapping the entire sky every six months, but until now, it lacked that same accessible, visual exploration tool. We want students, stargazers, and astronomers alike to explore this brand-new time-domain data stream and hunt for cold brown dwarfs, rogue asteroids, and elusive Planet X candidates as SPHEREx continues surveying our cosmic neighborhood.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use?

  • Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Astropy, Astroquery, PyVO, Reproject, and NumPy, Pandas
  • Frontend: Vanilla JavaScript, HTML5 Canvas, and modern CSS to keep performance snappy without framework bloat, paired with Aladin Lite (ESA HiPS) for sky navigation.
  • Data & Catalogs: NASA/IPAC IRSA (TAP/SIA APIs), AWS Open Data (nasa-irsa-spherex), CDS VizieR (reliable catalog mirror), Gaia DR3, and CatWISE2020 / AllWISE.
  • Infrastructure & Testing: Linux VPS with Nginx (https://blinkit.study), GitHub, Pytest (113 backend tests), and the Node test runner (62 frontend tests). We used coding assistants (Cursor) to accelerate repetitive test and boilerplate writing, while all core astronomy logic was checked against real archive data.

How our project is creative

Because SPHEREx uses Linear Variable Filters where the observed wavelength shifts continuously across each detector, blinking images taken at different times can create false visual illusions. We tackled this creatively by matching exposures with identical target wavelengths to ensure difference maps highlight true physical motion rather than instrument color shifts. We also turned multi-year observations into dynamic RGB color composites (where an object's drift leaves a distinct multi-color trail), and engineered automatic catalog fallbacks to CDS VizieR so the application never breaks even when NASA's IRSA TAP servers experience downtime.

What factors team considered?

Above all, we prioritized scientific honesty. We made sure our cleaning algorithms never mask out real celestial sources when removing instrument defects, any deviation of calculations, or mathematical methods that is needed most to truely get the essence of what we are building to know more about our space, adapted the interface to work smoothly on mobile phone screens, and built everything on real, unvarnished Level-2 NASA data rather than clean mockups. This hackathon is our starting point—we plan to keep maintaining and expanding Blinkit as new SPHEREx data releases continue to arrive.
